entities.name: Al-Azhar Great Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Great Mosque of Al-Azhar is the mosque component of the Al-Azhar complex in Cairo, representing the heart of Islamic learning and worship for over 1,050 years. While Al-Azhar Al-Sharif as an institutional entry covers the university-mosque complex broadly, the Great Mosque specifically refers to the prayer hall and architectural complex built from 970 CE onwards, which combines Fatimid, Mamluk, and Ottoman architectural elements in a palimpsest of Islamic history.

The original Fatimid mosque of 970-972 CE established the basic structure: a courtyard (sahn) surrounded by arcaded riwaqs on three sides and a five-aisled prayer hall on the qibla side, with the central aisle slightly wider and taller. Subsequent rulers added minarets, madrasas, and porticos, each in the prevailing style of their era — Mamluk minarets with their characteristic stalactite capitals, Ottoman additions after 1517, and modern 20th-century works.

The mosque's historical significance exceeds its current architectural state. Al-Azhar's Friday prayers are attended by thousands; the Grand Sheikh delivers sermons on matters of global Islamic importance. When Al-Azhar's Grand Sheikh Ahmed el-Tayeb condemned terrorism as un-Islamic, issued guidelines on treatment of religious minorities, or called for 'religious revolution' against extremism, he spoke from the pulpit of this mosque — giving his words authority drawn from 1,050 years of unbroken scholarly tradition. Al-Azhar's library, attached to the mosque, holds 12,000 manuscripts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Great Mosque of Al-Azhar is the world's most continuously significant mosque for Sunni Islam, its 1,050-year unbroken tradition of Friday prayers and scholarly authority making it the spiritual center of 1.8 billion Sunni Muslims.
